messages.text: Hi, I'm Kenji. I'm an NLP PhD student and I'm moving into HCI, and my project is about how non-experts write prompts for LLM tools. So, from this paper, what strategies did the non-AI experts actually use when they wrote prompts? Did they do something like trial and error, or was there a more systematic approach?

messages.short_answer: The passages provided describe the participants' approach only at a high level: they explored prompt designs opportunistically rather than systematically, and a tendency to overgeneralize and expectations from human-to-human instruction were barriers. The retrieved passages do not describe the specific strategies participants used, so the trial-and-error versus systematic question is only partly answered here.

sources.text: 2.2 Known Challenges in Prompt Design While prompting can appear as easy as instructing a human, crafting efective and generalizable prompt strategies is a challenging task. How a prompt or a prompt strategy directly impacts model outputs, and how prompts modify LLMs’ billions of parameters during re-training, are both active areas of NLP research [30, 42]. Moreover, established prompt design workfows do not yet exist. Even for NLP experts, prompt engineering requires extensive trial and error, iteratively experimenting and assessing the efects of various prompt strategies on concrete input-output pairs, before assessing them more systematically on large datasets. That said, ongoing NLP research does ofer some hints toward efective prompt design strategies. Notably, these prompt strategies are efective in improving LLMs’ performance over a range of NLP tasks and conversational contexts; it remains unclear to what extent these strategies can improve any particular conversational interactions or contexts.

messages.text: OK, so BotDesigner is the probe. Is that tool like a baseline model in my NLP sense, or more like the test set? Also, what exactly did that tool do for the participants?

messages.short_answer: BotDesigner is neither a baseline model nor a test set in the NLP sense. It is the design probe: a no-code prompt design tool that participants used to write and test chatbot prompts, and the researchers observed how they used it. The paper's "baseline" is a chatbot template that participants were asked to improve, not a model used for comparison.

sections.title: What the tool let participants do
sections.text: According to the passages, BotDesigner supports two activities: conversation authoring and interaction, where users instruct the chatbot with prompts alone and observe their effects in conversation, and error testing, where users collect conversations for each prompt draft, label errors, and inspect the overall impact in aggregate. The authors also say they did not necessarily expect all end-users to use every step.

sections.title: Why the tool is a probe, not a benchmark
sections.text: In NLP terms, a baseline model is a reference system you compare against, and a test set is data used to measure performance. The "baseline" in the paper refers to the starting chatbot template given to participants, which they were asked to improve.

Piloting your own tool would show whether the task is open enough to avoid a blank-page effect while still producing iteration.

sources.text: Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

These pages introduce BotDesigner, a React and node.js web application that uses OpenAI's GPT-3 text-davinci-002 model to help designers build prompt-based chatbots. The system offers a prompt template authoring area, a conversation authoring pane with labeling and retry features, and an Error Browser that tests a changed prompt template against all labeled bot responses across conversations. The authors justify choosing text-davinci-002 as the most capable instruction-following model available at the time, and they accept that cost and performance tradeoffs may change as newer models appear. An example walkthrough follows designer Alex, who creates a recipe-walkthrough chatbot for Mixed Veggie Tempura by writing a baseline prompt template and then testing it with sample user questions.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

Systematic testing and robust prompt design—designing prompts that work across many users and many conversations—are by defnition impossible if the user only ever engages in a single conversation, even continuously updated. That said, for some contexts non-robust prompt design can be appropriate: chatbots intended for a single user who is also the designer do not necessarily need to be robust. A second major opportunity stems from the fact that most of the prompt design approaches participants tried before receiving any guidance (see §3.3 for details regarding this guidance) had some efect—enough for participants to feel that they could, in fact, afect chatbot output with prompt changes—but participants hit dead ends that incurred interviewer intervention more frequently than we expected. A searchable repository of examples, such as The DALL·E 2 Prompt Book [37], could help users overcome the “design”, “selection”, and “use” barriers that often led to the aforementioned dead ends.
quotes: chatbots intended for a single user who is also the designer do not necessarily need to be robust.

sources.text: These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages, from the appendix of the paper, describe implementation details of BotDesigner, a tool for prompt-based chatbot design using GPT-3. The bot's responses are generated by concatenating a preamble, the conversation history with User and Bot prefixes, an optional reminder, and a final Bot prompt, sent to the text-davinci-002 model with temperature 0. The appendix explains two replay approaches for testing prompt changes, a "single replay" default chosen to reduce noise at the cost of accuracy, and a "total replay" approach aligned with regression testing. It also reports a small pilot with three academic researchers, who could detect most of five error categories in a baseline chatbot, and describes design changes made for the probe, such as dropping the Conversation Browser view.

- Writes in English with small grammar mistakes. Interface language: English.
